e-21598.knowledge_point: Evaluating Laplace Transforms of Constant Functions
e-21598.worked_solution:
For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $\mathcal L\{f(t)\}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s) = \mathcal L \{f(t)\} = \int_0^\infty e^{-st} f(t) \,\textrm d t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }2{e}^{-st}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }2{e}^{-st}\text{d}t \\  & =2{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s \neq 0$ or $s = 0.$

- If $s \neq 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =2{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t \\  & =2{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{2}{s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>0, \\ \infty ,\, & s<0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s = 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(0) & =2{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-0t}\text{d}t \\  & =2{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & =2{lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =2{lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & =2{lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s = 0,$ we have that $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{\infty} 2e^{-st} \textrm{d} t$ is divergent

- For $s > 0,$ we have that $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{\infty} 2e^{-st} \textrm{d} t$ is convergent

- For $s < 0,$ we have that $\displaystyle \int_{0}^{\infty} 2e^{-st} \textrm{d} t$ is divergent

Evaluating our integral for $s > 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =-\frac{2}{s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}-1) \\  & =-\frac{2}{s}(0-1) \\  & =\frac{2}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of $f(t)=2$ is $F(s) =\dfrac{2}{s},$ defined for $s > 0.$

e-21599.knowledge_point: Evaluating Laplace Transforms of Real Exponential Functions
e-21599.problem: Find the Laplace transform of $f(t) = e^{-2t}.$
e-21599.worked_solution:
For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $\mathcal L\{f(t)\}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s) = \mathcal L \{f(t)\} = 
\int_0^\infty e^{-st} f(t) \,\textrm d t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)=e^{-2t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-2t}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st-2t}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-2-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-2-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(-2-s)t}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s \neq -2$ or $s = -2.$

- If $s \neq -2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(-2-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{-2-s}{e}^{(-2-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{-2-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-2-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-2-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}-\frac{1}{s+2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-2-s)a}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-2-s)a}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>-2, \\ \infty ,\, & s<-2.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s = -2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(-2) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(-2-(-2))t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{0t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s \leq -2$ the integral is divergent.

- For $s > -2$ the integral is convergent.

Evaluating for $s > -2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s+2}-\frac{1}{s+2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-2-s)a} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}-\frac{1}{s+2}\cdot 0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the Laplace transform of $f(t)=e^{-2t}$ is $F(s) =\dfrac{1}{s+2},$ defined for $s > -2.$

e-21602.knowledge_point: Evaluating Laplace Transforms of Complex Exponentials
e-21602.problem: What is the Laplace transform of $f(t) = e^{2\textrm i t},$ where $t, s \in\mathbb  R?$
e-21602.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

For the function $f(t)=e^{2\textrm i t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{e}^{2\text{i}t}\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(2\text{i}-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating in the usual way, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(2\text{i}-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(2\text{i}-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{2\text{i}-s}{e}^{(2\text{i}-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(2\text{i}-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-2\text{i}}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(2\text{i}-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-2\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s-2\text{i}}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot {e}^{2\text{i}a}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall Euler's formula:

$$
e^{\textrm i\theta} = \cos\theta + \textrm i \sin\theta
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
F(s)= \dfrac{1}{s-2\textrm i} -  \dfrac{1}{s-2\textrm i}\left[\lim_{a\to \infty}e^{ -sa}\cdot \left(\cos(2a) + \textrm i\sin(2a)\right)  \right].
$$

Now, we have the following cases:

- For $s < 0,$ the term $e^{-sa}$ increases without bound while $\cos(2a) + \textrm i\sin(2a)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to\infty.$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s < 0.$

- For $s = 0,$ we have simply $\cos(2a) + \textrm i\sin(2a),$ which oscillates rapidly as $a\to\infty.$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s = 0.$

- For $s > 0,$ the term $e^{-sa}$ decays to zero while $\cos(2a) + \textrm i\sin(2a)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to\infty.$ Therefore, the limit of their product equals zero.

Therefore, for $s > 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s-2\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s-2\text{i}}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(2a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2a))] \\  & =\frac{1}{s-2\text{i}}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s-2\text{i}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of $e^{2\textrm i t}$ is $F(s) =\dfrac{1}{s-2\textrm i},$ defined for $s>0.$

EXPLANATION

For a function f(t) defined on [0,∞), the Laplace transform of f, denoted L{f(t)} or F(s), is a function of the variable s defined as F(s)=L{f(t)}=∫0∞e−stf(t)dt provided that this integral exists and is finite.

For the function f(t)=11, we have

F(s)=∫0∞11e−stdt.

We calculate our integral as follows: F(s)=∫0∞11e−stdt=11lima→∞∫0ae−stdt

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether s≠0 or s=0.

  • If s≠0, we have F(s)=11lima→∞∫0ae−stdt=11lima→∞(−1se−st)|0a=−11s(lima→∞e−sa−1). Let's evaluate the limit. We have lima→∞e−sa={0,s>0,∞,s<0.

  • If s=0, we have F(0)=11lima→∞∫0ae−0tdt=11lima→∞∫0adt=11lima→∞t|0a=11lima→∞(a−0)=11lima→∞a=∞.

Therefore:

  • For s>0, we have that ∫0∞11e−stdtis convergent

  • For s<0, we have that ∫0∞11e−stdtis divergent

  • For s=0, we have that ∫0∞11e−stdtis divergent

Evaluating our integral for s>0, we have

F(s)=−11s(lima→∞e−sa−1)=−11s(0−1)=11s.

So, the Laplace transform of f(t)=11 is F(s)=11s, defined for s>0.

decision.explanation: The Laplace definition gives ∫₀∞11e^{-st} dt. For s>0 this equals [-(11/s)e^{-st}]₀∞=11/s. For s<0 the integrand grows exponentially, and for s=0 it is constant; both cases diverge. Thus the transform is defined for s>0.

observation.worked_solution:
For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty ),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $L{f(t)}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)=11,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }11{e}^{-st}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }11{e}^{-st}\text{d}t \\  & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s\ne 0$ or $s=0.$

- If $s\ne 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t \\  & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{11}{s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>0, \\ \infty ,\, & s<0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(0) & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-0t}\text{d}t \\  & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s>0,$ we have that ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }11{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\,\text{is convergent}$

- For $s<0,$ we have that ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }11{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\,\text{is divergent}$

- For $s=0,$ we have that ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }11{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\,\text{is divergent}$

Evaluating our integral for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =-\frac{11}{s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}-1) \\  & =-\frac{11}{s}(0-1) \\  & =\frac{11}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of $f(t)=11$ is $F(s)=\frac{11}{s},$ defined for $s>0.$

after.worked_solution:
For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty ),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $L{f(t)}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)=11,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }11{e}^{-st}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }11{e}^{-st}\text{d}t \\  & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s\ne 0$ or $s=0.$

- If $s\ne 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t \\  & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{11}{s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>0, \\ \infty ,\, & s<0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(0) & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-0t}\text{d}t \\  & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s>0,$ we have that ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }11{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\,\text{is convergent}$

- For $s<0,$ we have that ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }11{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\,\text{is divergent}$

- For $s=0,$ we have that ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }11{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\,\text{is divergent}$

Evaluating our integral for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =-\frac{11}{s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}-1) \\  & =-\frac{11}{s}(0-1) \\  & =\frac{11}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of $f(t)=11$ is $F(s)=\frac{11}{s},$ defined for $s>0.$

content.worked_solution:
For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty ),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $L{f(t)}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)=11,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }11{e}^{-st}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }11{e}^{-st}\text{d}t \\  & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s\ne 0$ or $s=0.$

- If $s\ne 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t \\  & =11{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{11}{s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$

EXPLANATION

For a function f(t) defined on [0,∞), the Laplace transform of f, denoted L{f(t)} or F(s), is a function of the variable s defined as F(s)=L{f(t)}=∫0∞e−stf(t)dt provided that this integral exists and is finite.

For the function f(t)=−73, we have

F(s)=∫0∞−73e−stdt.

We calculate our integral as follows: F(s)=∫0∞−73e−stdt=−73lima→∞∫0ae−stdt

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether s≠0 or s=0.

  • If s≠0, we have F(s)=−73lima→∞∫0ae−stdt=−73lima→∞(−1se−st)|0a=73s(lima→∞e−sa−1). Let's evaluate the limit. We have lima→∞e−sa={0,s>0,∞,s<0.

  • If s=0, we have F(0)=−73lima→∞∫0ae−0tdt=−73lima→∞∫0adt=−73lima→∞t|0a=−73lima→∞(a−0)=−73lima→∞a=−∞.

Therefore:

  • For s<0, we have that ∫0∞−73e−stdtis divergent

  • For s>0, we have that ∫0∞−73e−stdtis convergent

  • For s=0, we have that ∫0∞−73e−stdtis divergent

Evaluating our integral for s>0, we have

F(s)=73s(lima→∞e−sa−1)=73s(0−1)=−73s.

So, the Laplace transform of f(t)=−73 is F(s)=−73s, defined for s>0.

decision.explanation: The Laplace definition gives ∫₀∞(-7/3)e^{-st} dt. For s>0, evaluating [7e^{-st}/(3s)]₀∞ yields -7/(3s). For s<0 the exponential grows, and for s=0 the integrand is a nonzero constant, so both integrals diverge. The domain is therefore s>0.

observation.worked_solution:
For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty ),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $L{f(t)}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)=-\frac{7}{3},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }-\frac{7}{3}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }-\frac{7}{3}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{7}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s\ne 0$ or $s=0.$

- If $s\ne 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =-\frac{7}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{7}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{7}{3s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>0, \\ \infty ,\, & s<0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(0) & =-\frac{7}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-0t}\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{7}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{7}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{7}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & =-\frac{7}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s<0,$ we have that ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }-\frac{7}{3}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\,\text{is divergent}$

- For $s>0,$ we have that ${\int }_{{}_{0}}^{\infty }-\frac{7}{3}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\,\text{is convergent}$

- For $s=0,$ we have that ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }-\frac{7}{3}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\,\text{is divergent}$

Evaluating our integral for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{7}{3s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}-1) \\  & =\frac{7}{3s}(0-1) \\  & =-\frac{7}{3s}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of $f(t)=-\frac{7}{3}$ is $F(s)=-\frac{7}{3s},$ defined for $s>0.$

For the function f(t)=−73, we have

F(s)=∫0∞−73e−stdt.

We calculate our integral as follows: F(s)=∫0∞−73e−stdt=−73lima→∞∫0ae−stdt

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether s≠0 or s=0.

Therefore:

  • For s<0, we have that ∫0∞−73e−stdtis divergent

  • For s>0, we have that ∫0∞−73e−stdtis convergent

  • For s=0, we have that ∫0∞−73e−stdtis divergent

after.worked_solution:
For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty ),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $L{f(t)}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)=-\frac{7}{3},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }-\frac{7}{3}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }-\frac{7}{3}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{7}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s\ne 0$ or $s=0.$

- If $s\ne 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =-\frac{7}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{7}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{7}{3s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>0, \\ \infty ,\, & s<0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(0) & =-\frac{7}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-0t}\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{7}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{7}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{7}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & =-\frac{7}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s<0,$ we have that ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }-\frac{7}{3}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\,\text{is divergent}$

- For $s>0,$ we have that ${\int }_{{}_{0}}^{\infty }-\frac{7}{3}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\,\text{is convergent}$

- For $s=0,$ we have that ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }-\frac{7}{3}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\,\text{is divergent}$

Evaluating our integral for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{7}{3s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}-1) \\  & =\frac{7}{3s}(0-1) \\  & =-\frac{7}{3s}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of $f(t)=-\frac{7}{3}$ is $F(s)=-\frac{7}{3s},$ defined for $s>0.$

For a function f(t) defined on [0,∞), the Laplace transform of f, denoted L{f(t)} or F(s), is a function of the variable s defined as F(s)=L{f(t)}=∫0∞e−stf(t)dt provided that this integral exists and is finite.

For the function f(t)=−73, we have

F(s)=∫0∞−73e−stdt.

We calculate our integral as follows: F(s)=∫0∞−73e−stdt=−73lima→∞∫0ae−stdt

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether s≠0 or s=0.

  • If s≠0, we have F(s)=−73lima→∞∫0ae−stdt=−73lima→∞(−1se−st)|0a=73s(lima→∞e−sa−1). Let's evaluate the limit. We have lima→∞e−sa={0,s>0,∞,s<0.

Therefore:

  • For s<0, we have that ∫0∞−73e−stdtis divergent

  • For s>0, we have that ∫0∞−73e−stdtis convergent

  • For s=0, we have that ∫0∞−73e−stdtis divergent

Evaluating our integral for s>0, we have

F(s)=73s(lima→∞e−sa−1)=73s(0−1)=−73s.

So, the Laplace transform of f(t)=−73 is F(s)=−73s, defined for s>0.

content.worked_solution:
For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty ),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $L{f(t)}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)=-\frac{7}{3},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }-\frac{7}{3}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }-\frac{7}{3}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{7}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s\ne 0$ or $s=0.$

- If $s\ne 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =-\frac{7}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{7}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(-\frac{1}{s}{e}^{-st})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{7}{3s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>0, \\ \infty ,\, & s<0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(0) & =-\frac{7}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-0t}\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{7}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{7}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{7}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & =-\frac{7}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s<0,$ we have that ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }-\frac{7}{3}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\,\text{is divergent}$

- For $s>0,$ we have that ${\int }_{{}_{0}}^{\infty }-\frac{7}{3}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\,\text{is convergent}$

- For $s=0,$ we have that ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }-\frac{7}{3}{e}^{-st}\text{d}t\,\text{is divergent}$

Evaluating our integral for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{7}{3s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}-1) \\  & =\frac{7}{3s}(0-1) \\  & =-\frac{7}{3s}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of $f(t)=-\frac{7}{3}$ is $F(s)=-\frac{7}{3s},$ defined for $s>0.$

before.worked_solution:
For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty ),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $L{f(t)}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)={e}^{7t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{7t}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st+7t}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(7-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(7-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(7-s)t}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s\ne 7$ or $s=7.$

- If $s\ne 7,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(7-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{7-s}{e}^{(7-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{7-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7}-\frac{1}{s-7}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7-s)a}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7-s)a}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>7, \\ \infty ,\, & s<7.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s=7,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(7) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(7-7)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{0t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s\le 7$ the integral is divergent.

- For $s>7$ the integral is convergent.

Evaluating for $s>7,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s-7}-\frac{1}{s-7}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7-s)a} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7}-\frac{1}{s-7}\cdot 0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{7t}$ is $F(s)=\frac{1}{s-7},$ defined for $s>7.$

EXPLANATION

For a function f(t) defined on [0,∞), the Laplace transform of f, denoted L{f(t)} or F(s), is a function of the variable s defined as F(s)=L{f(t)}=∫0∞e−stf(t)dt provided that this integral exists and is finite.

For the function f(t)=e7t, we have F(s)=∫0∞e−st⋅e7tdt=∫0∞e−st+7tdt=∫0∞e(7−s)tdt.

We calculate our integral as follows: F(s)=∫0∞e(7−s)tdt=lima→∞∫0ae(7−s)tdt

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether s≠7 or s=7.

  • If s≠7, we have F(s)=lima→∞∫0ae(7−s)tdt=lima→∞(17−se(7−s)t)|0a=17−s(lima→∞e(7−s)a−1)=1s−7(1−lima→∞e(7−s)a)=1s−7−1s−7⋅lima→∞e(7−s)a Let's evaluate the limit. We have lima→∞e(7−s)a={0,s>7,∞,s<7.

  • If s=7, we have F(7)=lima→∞∫0ae(7−7)tdt=lima→∞∫0ae0tdt=lima→∞∫0adt=lima→∞t|0a=lima→∞(a−0)=lima→∞a=∞.

Therefore:

  • For s≤7 the integral is divergent.

  • For s>7 the integral is convergent.

Evaluating for s>7, we have

F(s)=1s−7−1s−7⋅lima→∞e(7−s)a=1s−7−1s−7⋅0=1s−7.

So, the Laplace transform of f(t)=e7t is F(s)=1s−7, defined for s>7.

decision.explanation: The definition gives ∫₀∞e^{-st}e^{7t} dt=∫₀∞e^{(7-s)t} dt. It converges exactly when s>7, yielding [e^{(7-s)t}/(7-s)]₀∞=1/(s-7). For s≤7, the integrand grows or equals 1, so the integral diverges.

observation.worked_solution:
For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty ),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $L{f(t)}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)={e}^{7t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{7t}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st+7t}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(7-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(7-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(7-s)t}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s\ne 7$ or $s=7.$

- If $s\ne 7,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(7-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{7-s}{e}^{(7-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{7-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7}-\frac{1}{s-7}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7-s)a}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7-s)a}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>7, \\ \infty ,\, & s<7.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s=7,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(7) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(7-7)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{0t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s\le 7$ the integral is divergent.

- For $s>7$ the integral is convergent.

Evaluating for $s>7,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s-7}-\frac{1}{s-7}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7-s)a} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7}-\frac{1}{s-7}\cdot 0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{7t}$ is $F(s)=\frac{1}{s-7},$ defined for $s>7.$

EXPLANATION

For a function f(t) defined on [0,∞), the Laplace transform of f, denoted L{f(t)} or F(s), is a function of the variable s defined as F(s)=L{f(t)}=∫0∞e−stf(t)dt provided that this integral exists and is finite.

For the function f(t)=e7t, we have F(s)=∫0∞e−st⋅e7tdt=∫0∞e−st+7tdt=∫0∞e(7−s)tdt.

We calculate our integral as follows: F(s)=∫0∞e(7−s)tdt=lima→∞∫0ae(7−s)tdt

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether s≠7 or s=7.

  • If s≠7, we have F(s)=lima→∞∫0ae(7−s)tdt=lima→∞(17−se(7−s)t)|0a=17−s(lima→∞e(7−s)a−1)=1s−7(1−lima→∞e(7−s)a)=1s−7−1s−7⋅lima→∞e(7−s)a Let's evaluate the limit. We have lima→∞e(7−s)a={0,s>7,∞,s<7.

  • If s=7, we have F(7)=lima→∞∫0ae(7−7)tdt=lima→∞∫0ae0tdt=lima→∞∫0adt=lima→∞t|0a=lima→∞(a−0)=lima→∞a=∞.

Therefore:

  • For s≤7 the integral is divergent.

  • For s>7 the integral is convergent.

Evaluating for s>7, we have

F(s)=1s−7−1s−7⋅lima→∞e(7−s)a=1s−7−1s−7⋅0=1s−7.

So, the Laplace transform of f(t)=e7t is F(s)=1s−7, defined for s>7.

decision.explanation: The definition gives ∫₀∞e^{-st}e^{7t} dt=∫₀∞e^{(7-s)t} dt. It converges exactly when s>7, yielding [e^{(7-s)t}/(7-s)]₀∞=1/(s-7). For s≤7, the integrand grows or equals 1, so the integral diverges.

after.worked_solution:
For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty ),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $L{f(t)}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)={e}^{7t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{7t}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st+7t}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(7-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(7-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(7-s)t}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s\ne 7$ or $s=7.$

- If $s\ne 7,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(7-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{7-s}{e}^{(7-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{7-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7}-\frac{1}{s-7}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7-s)a}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7-s)a}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>7, \\ \infty ,\, & s<7.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s=7,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(7) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(7-7)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{0t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s\le 7$ the integral is divergent.

- For $s>7$ the integral is convergent.

Evaluating for $s>7,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s-7}-\frac{1}{s-7}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7-s)a} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7}-\frac{1}{s-7}\cdot 0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{7t}$ is $F(s)=\frac{1}{s-7},$ defined for $s>7.$

For a function f(t) defined on [0,∞), the Laplace transform of f, denoted L{f(t)} or F(s), is a function of the variable s defined as F(s)=L{f(t)}=∫0∞e−stf(t)dt provided that this integral exists and is finite.

  • If s≠7, we have F(s)=lima→∞∫0ae(7−s)tdt=lima→∞(17−se(7−s)t)|0a=17−s(lima→∞e(7−s)a−1)=1s−7(1−lima→∞e(7−s)a)=1s−7−1s−7⋅lima→∞e(7−s)a Let's evaluate the limit. We have lima→∞e(7−s)a={0,s>7,∞,s<7.

  • If s=7, we have F(7)=lima→∞∫0ae(7−7)tdt=lima→∞∫0ae0tdt=lima→∞∫0adt=lima→∞t|0a=lima→∞(a−0)=lima→∞a=∞.

Therefore:

Complete the arguments in the reasoning below to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{7t}.$First, we apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
L{f(t)}=F(s)={{field-1}}
$$

We now examine the convergence of $F(s)$ for different values of $s:$

$\,$ For {{field-2}}
the integral is divergent.

$\,$ For {{field-3}}
the integral is convergent.

Evaluating our integral in the convergent case, we have

$$

content.worked_solution:
For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty ),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $L{f(t)}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)={e}^{7t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{7t}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st+7t}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(7-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(7-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(7-s)t}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s\ne 7$ or $s=7.$

- If $s\ne 7,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(7-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{7-s}{e}^{(7-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{7-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7}-\frac{1}{s-7}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7-s)a}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7-s)a}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>7, \\ \infty ,\, & s<7.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s=7,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(7) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(7-7)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{0t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s\le 7$ the integral is divergent.

- For $s>7$ the integral is convergent.

Evaluating for $s>7,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s-7}-\frac{1}{s-7}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7-s)a} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7}-\frac{1}{s-7}\cdot 0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{7t}$ is $F(s)=\frac{1}{s-7},$ defined for $s>7.$

before.worked_solution:
For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty ),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $L{f(t)}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)={e}^{t/4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{t/4}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st+t/4}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s\ne \frac{1}{4}$ or $s=\frac{1}{4}.$

- If $s\ne \frac{1}{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{1/4-s}{e}^{(1/4-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{1/4-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}-\frac{1}{s-1/4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>\frac{1}{4}, \\ \infty ,\, & s<\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s=\frac{1}{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(\frac{1}{4}) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(1/4-1/4)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{0t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s>\frac{1}{4}$ the integral is convergent.

- For $s\le \frac{1}{4}$ the integral is divergent.

Evaluating for $s>\frac{1}{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}-\frac{1}{s-1/4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}-\frac{1}{s-1/4}\cdot 0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4} \\  & =\frac{4}{4s-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{t/4}$ is $F(s)=\frac{4}{4s-1},$ defined for $s>\frac{1}{4}.$

EXPLANATION

For a function f(t) defined on [0,∞), the Laplace transform of f, denoted L{f(t)} or F(s), is a function of the variable s defined as F(s)=L{f(t)}=∫0∞e−stf(t)dt provided that this integral exists and is finite.

For the function f(t)=et/4, we have F(s)=∫0∞e−st⋅et/4dt=∫0∞e−st+t/4dt=∫0∞e(1/4−s)tdt.

We calculate our integral as follows: F(s)=∫0∞e(1/4−s)tdt=lima→∞∫0ae(1/4−s)tdt

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether s≠14 or s=14.

  • If s≠14, we have F(s)=lima→∞∫0ae(1/4−s)tdt=lima→∞(11/4−se(1/4−s)t)|0a=11/4−s(lima→∞e(1/4−s)a−1)=1s−1/4(1−lima→∞e(1/4−s)a)=1s−1/4−1s−1/4⋅lima→∞e(1/4−s)a Let's evaluate the limit. We have lima→∞e(1/4−s)a={0,s>14,∞,s<14.

  • If s=14, we have F(14)=lima→∞∫0ae(1/4−1/4)tdt=lima→∞∫0ae0tdt=lima→∞∫0adt=lima→∞t|0a=lima→∞(a−0)=lima→∞a=∞.

Therefore:

  • For s>14 the integral is convergent.

  • For s≤14 the integral is divergent.

Evaluating for s>14, we have

F(s)=1s−1/4−1s−1/4⋅lima→∞e(1/4−s)a=1s−1/4−1s−1/4⋅0=1s−1/4=44s−1.

So, the Laplace transform of f(t)=et/4 is F(s)=44s−1, defined for s>14.

decision.explanation: The definition gives ∫₀∞e^{-st}e^{t/4} dt=∫₀∞e^{(1/4-s)t} dt. This converges exactly for s>1/4, with value 1/(s-1/4)=4/(4s-1). For s≤1/4 the integrand grows or equals 1, so the integral diverges.

Question 4
?
Complete the arguments in the reasoning below to find the Laplace transform of f(t)=et/4.First, we apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

∫−∞∞e(1/4+s)tdt
∫−∞∞e(1/4−s)tdt
∫0∞e(1/4+s)tdt
∫0∞e(1/4−s)tdt
∫−∞∞e(1/4+s)tdt
L{f(t)}=F(s)={(∫−∞∞e(1/4−s)tdt)(S0)}

$$
L{f(t)}=F(s)={{field-1}}
$$

We now examine the convergence of $F(s)$ for different values of $s:$

$\,$ For {{field-2}}
the integral is convergent.

$\,$ For {{field-3}}
the integral is divergent.

Evaluating our integral in the convergent case, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\,\text{d}t={{field-4}}.
$$

decision.explanation: The Laplace integrand is e^{-st}e^{t/4}=e^{(1/4-s)t}. The integral converges when 1/4-s<0, or s>1/4. For s<1/4 it grows exponentially, and at s=1/4 it equals 1, so it diverges for s≤1/4.

observation.worked_solution:
For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty ),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $L{f(t)}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)={e}^{t/4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{t/4}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st+t/4}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s\ne \frac{1}{4}$ or $s=\frac{1}{4}.$

- If $s\ne \frac{1}{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{1/4-s}{e}^{(1/4-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{1/4-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}-\frac{1}{s-1/4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>\frac{1}{4}, \\ \infty ,\, & s<\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s=\frac{1}{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(\frac{1}{4}) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(1/4-1/4)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{0t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s>\frac{1}{4}$ the integral is convergent.

- For $s\le \frac{1}{4}$ the integral is divergent.

Evaluating for $s>\frac{1}{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}-\frac{1}{s-1/4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}-\frac{1}{s-1/4}\cdot 0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4} \\  & =\frac{4}{4s-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{t/4}$ is $F(s)=\frac{4}{4s-1},$ defined for $s>\frac{1}{4}.$

For a function f(t) defined on [0,∞), the Laplace transform of f, denoted L{f(t)} or F(s), is a function of the variable s defined as F(s)=L{f(t)}=∫0∞e−stf(t)dt provided that this integral exists and is finite.

For the function f(t)=et/4, we have F(s)=∫0∞e−st⋅et/4dt=∫0∞e−st+t/4dt=∫0∞e(1/4−s)tdt.

We calculate our integral as follows: F(s)=∫0∞e(1/4−s)tdt=lima→∞∫0ae(1/4−s)tdt

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether s≠14 or s=14.

  • If s≠14, we have F(s)=lima→∞∫0ae(1/4−s)tdt=lima→∞(11/4−se(1/4−s)t)|0a=11/4−s(lima→∞e(1/4−s)a−1)=1s−1/4(1−lima→∞e(1/4−s)a)=1s−1/4−1s−1/4⋅lima→∞e(1/4−s)a Let's evaluate the limit. We have lima→∞e(1/4−s)a={0,s>14,∞,s<14.

  • If s=14, we have F(14)=lima→∞∫0ae(1/4−1/4)tdt=lima→∞∫0ae0tdt=lima→∞∫0adt=lima→∞t|0a=lima→∞(a−0)=lima→∞a=∞.

Therefore:

  • For s>14 the integral is convergent.

  • For s≤14 the integral is divergent.

Evaluating for s>14, we have

F(s)=1s−1/4−1s−1/4⋅lima→∞e(1/4−s)a=1s−1/4−1s−1/4⋅0=1s−1/4=44s−1.

So, the Laplace transform of f(t)=et/4 is F(s)=44s−1, defined for s>14.

after.worked_solution:
For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty ),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $L{f(t)}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)={e}^{t/4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{t/4}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st+t/4}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s\ne \frac{1}{4}$ or $s=\frac{1}{4}.$

- If $s\ne \frac{1}{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{1/4-s}{e}^{(1/4-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{1/4-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}-\frac{1}{s-1/4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>\frac{1}{4}, \\ \infty ,\, & s<\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s=\frac{1}{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(\frac{1}{4}) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(1/4-1/4)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{0t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s>\frac{1}{4}$ the integral is convergent.

- For $s\le \frac{1}{4}$ the integral is divergent.

Evaluating for $s>\frac{1}{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}-\frac{1}{s-1/4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}-\frac{1}{s-1/4}\cdot 0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4} \\  & =\frac{4}{4s-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{t/4}$ is $F(s)=\frac{4}{4s-1},$ defined for $s>\frac{1}{4}.$

EXPLANATION

For a function f(t) defined on [0,∞), the Laplace transform of f, denoted L{f(t)} or F(s), is a function of the variable s defined as F(s)=L{f(t)}=∫0∞e−stf(t)dt provided that this integral exists and is finite.

For the function f(t)=et/4, we have F(s)=∫0∞e−st⋅et/4dt=∫0∞e−st+t/4dt=∫0∞e(1/4−s)tdt.

We calculate our integral as follows: F(s)=∫0∞e(1/4−s)tdt=lima→∞∫0ae(1/4−s)tdt

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether s≠14 or s=14.

  • If s≠14, we have F(s)=lima→∞∫0ae(1/4−s)tdt=lima→∞(11/4−se(1/4−s)t)|0a=11/4−s(lima→∞e(1/4−s)a−1)=1s−1/4(1−lima→∞e(1/4−s)a)=1s−1/4−1s−1/4⋅lima→∞e(1/4−s)a Let's evaluate the limit. We have lima→∞e(1/4−s)a={0,s>14,∞,s<14.

  • If s=14, we have F(14)=lima→∞∫0ae(1/4−1/4)tdt=lima→∞∫0ae0tdt=lima→∞∫0adt=lima→∞t|0a=lima→∞(a−0)=lima→∞a=∞.

Therefore:

  • For s>14 the integral is convergent.

  • For s≤14 the integral is divergent.

Evaluating for s>14, we have

F(s)=1s−1/4−1s−1/4⋅lima→∞e(1/4−s)a=1s−1/4−1s−1/4⋅0=1s−1/4=44s−1.

So, the Laplace transform of f(t)=et/4 is F(s)=44s−1, defined for s>14.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms the answers: e^{-st}e^{t/4}=e^{(1/4-s)t}, which is integrable exactly for s>1/4. Its integral is 1/(s-1/4)=4/(4s-1). At s=1/4 the integrand equals 1, and below that it grows, so the integral diverges for s≤1/4.

content.worked_solution:
For a function $f(t)$ defined on $[0,\infty ),$ the Laplace transform of $f,$ denoted $L{f(t)}$ or $F(s),$ is a function of the variable $s$ defined as

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

provided that this integral exists and is finite. 

For the function $f(t)={e}^{t/4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{t/4}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st+t/4}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

To evaluate the last integral, we must consider whether $s\ne \frac{1}{4}$ or $s=\frac{1}{4}.$

- If $s\ne \frac{1}{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(1/4-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{1/4-s}{e}^{(1/4-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{1/4-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}-\frac{1}{s-1/4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's evaluate the limit. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a}={\begin{aligned}0,\, & s>\frac{1}{4}, \\ \infty ,\, & s<\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

- If $s=\frac{1}{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(\frac{1}{4}) & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(1/4-1/4)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{0t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }t\,{|}_{0}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(a-0) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }a \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- For $s>\frac{1}{4}$ the integral is convergent.

- For $s\le \frac{1}{4}$ the integral is divergent.

Evaluating for $s>\frac{1}{4},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}-\frac{1}{s-1/4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(1/4-s)a} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4}-\frac{1}{s-1/4}\cdot 0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s-1/4} \\  & =\frac{4}{4s-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{t/4}$ is $F(s)=\frac{4}{4s-1},$ defined for $s>\frac{1}{4}.$

decision.explanation: Integrating e^{-(s+i/9)t} from 0 to infinity gives 1/(s+i/9)=9/(9s+i). For real s, the exponential decays exactly when s>0; for s≤0 the improper integral does not converge.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
What is the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{-\text{i}t/9},$ where $t,s\in R?$$\,L(f(t))=$
{{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
after.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

For the function $f(t)={e}^{-\text{i}t/9},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{e}^{-\text{i}t/9}\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-\text{i}/9-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating in the usual way, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-\text{i}/9-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(-\text{i}/9-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{-\text{i}/9-s}{e}^{(-\text{i}/9-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{-\text{i}/9-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-\text{i}/9-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-\text{i}/9-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}-\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot {e}^{-\text{i}a/9}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall Euler's formula:

$$
{e}^{\text{i}\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}-\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(-a/9)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-a/9))].
$$

Now, we have the following cases:

- For $s<0,$ the term ${e}^{-sa}$ increases without bound while $\operatorname{cos}⁡(-a/9)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-a/9)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s<0.$

- For $s=0,$ we have simply $\operatorname{cos}⁡(-a/9)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-a/9),$ which oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s=0.$

- For $s>0,$ the term ${e}^{-sa}$ decays to zero while $\operatorname{cos}⁡(-a/9)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-a/9)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit of their product equals zero.

Therefore, for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}-\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(-a/9)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-a/9))] \\  & =\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9} \\  & =\frac{9}{9s+\text{i}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of ${e}^{-\text{i}t/9}$ is $F(s)=\frac{9}{9s+\text{i}},$ defined for $s>0.$

EXPLANATION

We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

L{f(t)}=F(s)=∫0∞e−stf(t)dt

For the function f(t)=e−it/9, we have

F(s)=∫0∞e−ste−it/9dt=∫0∞e(−i/9−s)tdt.

Evaluating in the usual way, we have

F(s)=∫0∞e(−i/9−s)tdt=lima→∞∫0ae(−i/9−s)tdt=lima→∞(1−i/9−se(−i/9−s)t)|0a=1−i/9−s(lima→∞e(−i/9−s)a−1)=1s+i/9(1−lima→∞e(−i/9−s)a)=1s+i/9−1s+i/9(lima→∞e−sa⋅e−ia/9).

Now, we recall Euler's formula:

eiθ=cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ

Therefore, we have

F(s)=1s+i/9−1s+i/9[lima→∞e−sa⋅(cos⁡(−a/9)+isin⁡(−a/9))].

Now, we have the following cases:

  • For s<0, the term e−sa increases without bound while cos⁡(−a/9)+isin⁡(−a/9) oscillates rapidly as a→∞. Therefore, the limit does not exist for s<0.

  • For s=0, we have simply cos⁡(−a/9)+isin⁡(−a/9), which oscillates rapidly as a→∞. Therefore, the limit does not exist for s=0.

  • For s>0, the term e−sa decays to zero while cos⁡(−a/9)+isin⁡(−a/9) oscillates rapidly as a→∞. Therefore, the limit of their product equals zero.

Therefore, for s>0, we have

F(s)=1s+i/9−1s+i/9[lima→∞e−sa⋅(cos⁡(−a/9)+isin⁡(−a/9))]=1s+i/9−0=1s+i/9=99s+i.

So, the Laplace transform of e−it/9 is F(s)=99s+i, defined for s>0.

content.problem:
What is the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{-\text{i}t/9},$ where $t,s\in R?$$\,L(f(t))=$
{{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
content.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

For the function $f(t)={e}^{-\text{i}t/9},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{e}^{-\text{i}t/9}\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-\text{i}/9-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating in the usual way, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-\text{i}/9-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(-\text{i}/9-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{-\text{i}/9-s}{e}^{(-\text{i}/9-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{-\text{i}/9-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-\text{i}/9-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-\text{i}/9-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}-\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot {e}^{-\text{i}a/9}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall Euler's formula:

$$
{e}^{\text{i}\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}-\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(-a/9)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-a/9))].
$$

Now, we have the following cases:

- For $s<0,$ the term ${e}^{-sa}$ increases without bound while $\operatorname{cos}⁡(-a/9)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-a/9)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s<0.$

- For $s=0,$ we have simply $\operatorname{cos}⁡(-a/9)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-a/9),$ which oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s=0.$

- For $s>0,$ the term ${e}^{-sa}$ decays to zero while $\operatorname{cos}⁡(-a/9)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-a/9)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit of their product equals zero.

Therefore, for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}-\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(-a/9)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-a/9))] \\  & =\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9} \\  & =\frac{9}{9s+\text{i}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of ${e}^{-\text{i}t/9}$ is $F(s)=\frac{9}{9s+\text{i}},$ defined for $s>0.$

history.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

For the function $f(t)={e}^{-\text{i}t/9},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{e}^{-\text{i}t/9}\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-\text{i}/9-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating in the usual way, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-\text{i}/9-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(-\text{i}/9-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{-\text{i}/9-s}{e}^{(-\text{i}/9-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{-\text{i}/9-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-\text{i}/9-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-\text{i}/9-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}-\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot {e}^{-\text{i}a/9}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall Euler's formula:

$$
{e}^{\text{i}\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}-\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(-a/9)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-a/9))].
$$

Now, we have the following cases:

- For $s<0,$ the term ${e}^{-sa}$ increases without bound while $\operatorname{cos}⁡(-a/9)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-a/9)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s<0.$

- For $s=0,$ we have simply $\operatorname{cos}⁡(-a/9)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-a/9),$ which oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s=0.$

- For $s>0,$ the term ${e}^{-sa}$ decays to zero while $\operatorname{cos}⁡(-a/9)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-a/9)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit of their product equals zero.

Therefore, for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}-\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(-a/9)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-a/9))] \\  & =\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s+\text{i}/9} \\  & =\frac{9}{9s+\text{i}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of ${e}^{-\text{i}t/9}$ is $F(s)=\frac{9}{9s+\text{i}},$ defined for $s>0.$

We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

L{f(t)}=F(s)=∫0∞e−stf(t)dt

For the function f(t)=e−it/9, we have

F(s)=∫0∞e−ste−it/9dt=∫0∞e(−i/9−s)tdt.

Evaluating in the usual way, we have

F(s)=∫0∞e(−i/9−s)tdt=lima→∞∫0ae(−i/9−s)tdt=lima→∞(1−i/9−se(−i/9−s)t)|0a=1−i/9−s(lima→∞e(−i/9−s)a−1)=1s+i/9(1−lima→∞e(−i/9−s)a)=1s+i/9−1s+i/9(lima→∞e−sa⋅e−ia/9).

Now, we recall Euler's formula:

eiθ=cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ

Therefore, we have

F(s)=1s+i/9−1s+i/9[lima→∞e−sa⋅(cos⁡(−a/9)+isin⁡(−a/9))].

Now, we have the following cases:

  • For s<0, the term e−sa increases without bound while cos⁡(−a/9)+isin⁡(−a/9) oscillates rapidly as a→∞. Therefore, the limit does not exist for s<0.

  • For s=0, we have simply cos⁡(−a/9)+isin⁡(−a/9), which oscillates rapidly as a→∞. Therefore, the limit does not exist for s=0.

  • For s>0, the term e−sa decays to zero while cos⁡(−a/9)+isin⁡(−a/9) oscillates rapidly as a→∞. Therefore, the limit of their product equals zero.

Therefore, for s>0, we have

F(s)=1s+i/9−1s+i/9[lima→∞e−sa⋅(cos⁡(−a/9)+isin⁡(−a/9))]=1s+i/9−0=1s+i/9=99s+i.

So, the Laplace transform of e−it/9 is F(s)=99s+i, defined for s>0.

decision.explanation: The Laplace integral is ∫₀∞e^{-(s-4i)t} dt=1/(s-4i). For real s, it converges exactly when s>0 because the factor e^{-st} decays; for s≤0 the boundary term has no limit.

after.problem:

{{field-1}},

after.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

For the function $f(t)={e}^{4\text{i}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{e}^{4\text{i}t}\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(4\text{i}-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating in the usual way, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(4\text{i}-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(4\text{i}-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{4\text{i}-s}{e}^{(4\text{i}-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\text{i}-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(4\text{i}-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-4\text{i}}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(4\text{i}-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-4\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s-4\text{i}}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot {e}^{4\text{i}a}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall Euler's formula:

$$
{e}^{\text{i}\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{s-4\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s-4\text{i}}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(4a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4a))].
$$

Now, we have the following cases:

- For $s<0,$ the term ${e}^{-sa}$ increases without bound while $\operatorname{cos}⁡(4a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4a)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s<0.$

- For $s=0,$ we have simply $\operatorname{cos}⁡(4a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4a),$ which oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s=0.$

- For $s>0,$ the term ${e}^{-sa}$ decays to zero while $\operatorname{cos}⁡(4a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4a)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit of their product equals zero.

Therefore, for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s-4\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s-4\text{i}}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(4a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4a))] \\  & =\frac{1}{s-4\text{i}}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s-4\text{i}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of ${e}^{4\text{i}t}$ is $F(s)=\frac{1}{s-4\text{i}},$ defined for $s>0.$

EXPLANATION

We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

L{f(t)}=F(s)=∫0∞e−stf(t)dt

For the function f(t)=e4it, we have

F(s)=∫0∞e−ste4itdt=∫0∞e(4i−s)tdt.

Evaluating in the usual way, we have

F(s)=∫0∞e(4i−s)tdt=lima→∞∫0ae(4i−s)tdt=lima→∞(14i−se(4i−s)t)|0a=14i−s(lima→∞e(4i−s)a−1)=1s−4i(1−lima→∞e(4i−s)a)=1s−4i−1s−4i(lima→∞e−sa⋅e4ia).

Now, we recall Euler's formula:

eiθ=cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ

Therefore, we have

F(s)=1s−4i−1s−4i[lima→∞e−sa⋅(cos⁡(4a)+isin⁡(4a))].

Now, we have the following cases:

  • For s<0, the term e−sa increases without bound while cos⁡(4a)+isin⁡(4a) oscillates rapidly as a→∞. Therefore, the limit does not exist for s<0.

  • For s=0, we have simply cos⁡(4a)+isin⁡(4a), which oscillates rapidly as a→∞. Therefore, the limit does not exist for s=0.

  • For s>0, the term e−sa decays to zero while cos⁡(4a)+isin⁡(4a) oscillates rapidly as a→∞. Therefore, the limit of their product equals zero.

Therefore, for s>0, we have

F(s)=1s−4i−1s−4i[lima→∞e−sa⋅(cos⁡(4a)+isin⁡(4a))]=1s−4i−0=1s−4i.

So, the Laplace transform of e4it is F(s)=1s−4i, defined for s>0.

content.problem:
What is the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{4\text{i}t},$ where $t,s\in R?$$\,L(f(t))=$
{{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
content.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

For the function $f(t)={e}^{4\text{i}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{e}^{4\text{i}t}\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(4\text{i}-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating in the usual way, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(4\text{i}-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(4\text{i}-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{4\text{i}-s}{e}^{(4\text{i}-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\text{i}-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(4\text{i}-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-4\text{i}}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(4\text{i}-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-4\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s-4\text{i}}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot {e}^{4\text{i}a}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall Euler's formula:

$$
{e}^{\text{i}\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{s-4\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s-4\text{i}}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(4a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4a))].
$$

Now, we have the following cases:

- For $s<0,$ the term ${e}^{-sa}$ increases without bound while $\operatorname{cos}⁡(4a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4a)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s<0.$

- For $s=0,$ we have simply $\operatorname{cos}⁡(4a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4a),$ which oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s=0.$

- For $s>0,$ the term ${e}^{-sa}$ decays to zero while $\operatorname{cos}⁡(4a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4a)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit of their product equals zero.

Therefore, for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s-4\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s-4\text{i}}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(4a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4a))] \\  & =\frac{1}{s-4\text{i}}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s-4\text{i}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of ${e}^{4\text{i}t}$ is $F(s)=\frac{1}{s-4\text{i}},$ defined for $s>0.$

\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

For the function $f(t)={e}^{7\text{i}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{e}^{7\text{i}t}\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(7\text{i}-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating in the usual way, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(7\text{i}-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(7\text{i}-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{7\text{i}-s}{e}^{(7\text{i}-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{7\text{i}-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7\text{i}-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7\text{i}}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7\text{i}-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s-7\text{i}}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot {e}^{7\text{i}a}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall Euler's formula:

$$
{e}^{\text{i}\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{s-7\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s-7\text{i}}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(7a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7a))].
$$

Now, we have the following cases:

- For $s<0,$ the term ${e}^{-sa}$ increases without bound while $\operatorname{cos}⁡(7a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7a)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s<0.$

- For $s=0,$ we have simply $\operatorname{cos}⁡(7a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7a),$ which oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s=0.$

- For $s>0,$ the term ${e}^{-sa}$ decays to zero while $\operatorname{cos}⁡(7a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7a)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit of their product equals zero.

Therefore, for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s-7\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s-7\text{i}}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(7a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7a))] \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7\text{i}}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7\text{i}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of ${e}^{7\text{i}t}$ is $F(s)=\frac{1}{s-7\text{i}},$ defined for $s>0.$

EXPLANATION

We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

L{f(t)}=F(s)=∫0∞e−stf(t)dt

For the function f(t)=e7it, we have

F(s)=∫0∞e−ste7itdt=∫0∞e(7i−s)tdt.

Evaluating in the usual way, we have

F(s)=∫0∞e(7i−s)tdt=lima→∞∫0ae(7i−s)tdt=lima→∞(17i−se(7i−s)t)|0a=17i−s(lima→∞e(7i−s)a−1)=1s−7i(1−lima→∞e(7i−s)a)=1s−7i−1s−7i(lima→∞e−sa⋅e7ia).

Now, we recall Euler's formula:

eiθ=cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ

Therefore, we have

F(s)=1s−7i−1s−7i[lima→∞e−sa⋅(cos⁡(7a)+isin⁡(7a))].

Now, we have the following cases:

  • For s<0, the term e−sa increases without bound while cos⁡(7a)+isin⁡(7a) oscillates rapidly as a→∞. Therefore, the limit does not exist for s<0.

  • For s=0, we have simply cos⁡(7a)+isin⁡(7a), which oscillates rapidly as a→∞. Therefore, the limit does not exist for s=0.

  • For s>0, the term e−sa decays to zero while cos⁡(7a)+isin⁡(7a) oscillates rapidly as a→∞. Therefore, the limit of their product equals zero.

Therefore, for s>0, we have

F(s)=1s−7i−1s−7i[lima→∞e−sa⋅(cos⁡(7a)+isin⁡(7a))]=1s−7i−0=1s−7i.

So, the Laplace transform of e7it is F(s)=1s−7i, defined for s>0.

content.problem:
What is the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{7\text{i}t},$ where $t,s\in R?$$\,L(f(t))=$
{{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
content.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

For the function $f(t)={e}^{7\text{i}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{e}^{7\text{i}t}\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(7\text{i}-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating in the usual way, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(7\text{i}-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(7\text{i}-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{7\text{i}-s}{e}^{(7\text{i}-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{7\text{i}-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7\text{i}-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7\text{i}}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(7\text{i}-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s-7\text{i}}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot {e}^{7\text{i}a}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall Euler's formula:

$$
{e}^{\text{i}\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{s-7\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s-7\text{i}}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(7a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7a))].
$$

Now, we have the following cases:

- For $s<0,$ the term ${e}^{-sa}$ increases without bound while $\operatorname{cos}⁡(7a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7a)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s<0.$

- For $s=0,$ we have simply $\operatorname{cos}⁡(7a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7a),$ which oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s=0.$

- For $s>0,$ the term ${e}^{-sa}$ decays to zero while $\operatorname{cos}⁡(7a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7a)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit of their product equals zero.

Therefore, for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s-7\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s-7\text{i}}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(7a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7a))] \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7\text{i}}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s-7\text{i}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of ${e}^{7\text{i}t}$ is $F(s)=\frac{1}{s-7\text{i}},$ defined for $s>0.$

$$

For the function f(t)=e7it, we have

F(s)=∫0∞e−ste7itdt=∫0∞e(7i−s)tdt.

Evaluating in the usual way, we have

F(s)=∫0∞e(7i−s)tdt=lima→∞∫0ae(7i−s)tdt=lima→∞(17i−se(7i−s)t)|0a=17i−s(lima→∞e(7i−s)a−1)=1s−7i(1−lima→∞e(7i−s)a)=1s−7i−1s−7i(lima→∞e−sa⋅e7ia).

Now, we recall Euler's formula:

eiθ=cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ

Therefore, we have

F(s)=1s−7i−1s−7i[lima→∞e−sa⋅(cos⁡(7a)+isin⁡(7a))].

Now, we have the following cases:

  • For s<0, the term e−sa increases without bound while cos⁡(7a)+isin⁡(7a) oscillates rapidly as a→∞. Therefore, the limit does not exist for s<0.

  • For s=0, we have simply cos⁡(7a)+isin⁡(7a), which oscillates rapidly as a→∞. Therefore, the limit does not exist for s=0.

  • For s>0, the term e−sa decays to zero while cos⁡(7a)+isin⁡(7a) oscillates rapidly as a→∞. Therefore, the limit of their product equals zero.

F(s)=1s−7i−1s−7i[lima→∞e−sa⋅(cos⁡(7a)+isin⁡(7a))]=1s−7i−0=1s−7i.

decision.explanation: The Laplace integral is ∫₀∞e^{-(s+3i/8)t} dt=1/(s+3i/8)=8/(8s+3i). For real s, it converges exactly when s>0; for s≤0 the boundary term has no limit.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
What is the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{-3\text{i}t/8},$ where $t,s\in R?$$\,L(f(t))=$
{{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
after.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

For the function $f(t)={e}^{-3\text{i}t/8},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{e}^{-3\text{i}t/8}\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-3\text{i}/8-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating in the usual way, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-3\text{i}/8-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(-3\text{i}/8-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{-3\text{i}/8-s}{e}^{(-3\text{i}/8-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{-3\text{i}/8-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-3\text{i}/8-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-3\text{i}/8-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8}-\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot {e}^{-3\text{i}a/8}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall Euler's formula:

$$
{e}^{\text{i}\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8}-\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3a/8)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-3a/8))].
$$

Now, we have the following cases:

- For $s<0,$ the term ${e}^{-sa}$ increases without bound while $\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3a/8)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-3a/8)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s<0.$

- For $s=0,$ we have simply $\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3a/8)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-3a/8),$ which oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s=0.$

- For $s>0,$ the term ${e}^{-sa}$ decays to zero while $\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3a/8)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-3a/8)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit of their product equals zero.

Therefore, for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8}-\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3a/8)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-3a/8))] \\  & =\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8} \\  & =\frac{8}{8s+3\text{i}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of ${e}^{-3\text{i}t/8}$ is $F(s)=\frac{8}{8s+3\text{i}},$ defined for $s>0.$

Correct
EXPLANATION

We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

L{f(t)}=F(s)=∫0∞e−stf(t)dt

For the function f(t)=e−3it/8, we have

F(s)=∫0∞e−ste−3it/8dt=∫0∞e(−3i/8−s)tdt.

Evaluating in the usual way, we have

F(s)=∫0∞e(−3i/8−s)tdt=lima→∞∫0ae(−3i/8−s)tdt=lima→∞(1−3i/8−se(−3i/8−s)t)|0a=1−3i/8−s(lima→∞e(−3i/8−s)a−1)=1s+3i/8(1−lima→∞e(−3i/8−s)a)=1s+3i/8−1s+3i/8(lima→∞e−sa⋅e−3ia/8).

Now, we recall Euler's formula:

eiθ=cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ

Therefore, we have

F(s)=1s+3i/8−1s+3i/8[lima→∞e−sa⋅(cos⁡(−3a/8)+isin⁡(−3a/8))].

Now, we have the following cases:

  • For s<0, the term e−sa increases without bound while cos⁡(−3a/8)+isin⁡(−3a/8) oscillates rapidly as a→∞. Therefore, the limit does not exist for s<0.

  • For s=0, we have simply cos⁡(−3a/8)+isin⁡(−3a/8), which oscillates rapidly as a→∞. Therefore, the limit does not exist for s=0.

  • For s>0, the term e−sa decays to zero while cos⁡(−3a/8)+isin⁡(−3a/8) oscillates rapidly as a→∞. Therefore, the limit of their product equals zero.

Therefore, for s>0, we have

F(s)=1s+3i/8−1s+3i/8[lima→∞e−sa⋅(cos⁡(−3a/8)+isin⁡(−3a/8))]=1s+3i/8−0=1s+3i/8=88s+3i.

So, the Laplace transform of e−3it/8 is F(s)=88s+3i, defined for s>0.

content.problem:
What is the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{-3\text{i}t/8},$ where $t,s\in R?$$\,L(f(t))=$
{{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
content.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

For the function $f(t)={e}^{-3\text{i}t/8},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{e}^{-3\text{i}t/8}\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-3\text{i}/8-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating in the usual way, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-3\text{i}/8-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(-3\text{i}/8-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{-3\text{i}/8-s}{e}^{(-3\text{i}/8-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{-3\text{i}/8-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-3\text{i}/8-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-3\text{i}/8-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8}-\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot {e}^{-3\text{i}a/8}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall Euler's formula:

$$
{e}^{\text{i}\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8}-\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3a/8)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-3a/8))].
$$

Now, we have the following cases:

- For $s<0,$ the term ${e}^{-sa}$ increases without bound while $\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3a/8)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-3a/8)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s<0.$

- For $s=0,$ we have simply $\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3a/8)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-3a/8),$ which oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s=0.$

- For $s>0,$ the term ${e}^{-sa}$ decays to zero while $\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3a/8)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-3a/8)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit of their product equals zero.

Therefore, for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8}-\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3a/8)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-3a/8))] \\  & =\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s+3\text{i}/8} \\  & =\frac{8}{8s+3\text{i}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of ${e}^{-3\text{i}t/8}$ is $F(s)=\frac{8}{8s+3\text{i}},$ defined for $s>0.$

decision.explanation: The Laplace integral is ∫₀∞e^{-(s+2i)t} dt=1/(s+2i). For real s, it converges exactly when s>0 because e^{-st} decays; for s≤0 the boundary term has no limit.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
What is the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{-2\text{i}t},$ where $t,s\in R?$$\,L(f(t))=$
{{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
after.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

For the function $f(t)={e}^{-2\text{i}t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}{e}^{-2\text{i}t}\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-2\text{i}-s)t}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating in the usual way, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{(-2\text{i}-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{(-2\text{i}-s)t}\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{-2\text{i}-s}{e}^{(-2\text{i}-s)t})|}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{-2\text{i}-s}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-2\text{i}-s)a}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2\text{i}}(1-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{(-2\text{i}-s)a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s+2\text{i}}({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot {e}^{-2\text{i}a}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall Euler's formula:

$$
{e}^{\text{i}\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
F(s)=\frac{1}{s+2\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s+2\text{i}}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(-2a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-2a))].
$$

Now, we have the following cases:

- For $s<0,$ the term ${e}^{-sa}$ increases without bound while $\operatorname{cos}⁡(-2a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-2a)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s<0.$

- For $s=0,$ we have simply $\operatorname{cos}⁡(-2a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-2a),$ which oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit does not exist for $s=0.$

- For $s>0,$ the term ${e}^{-sa}$ decays to zero while $\operatorname{cos}⁡(-2a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-2a)$ oscillates rapidly as $a\to \infty .$ Therefore, the limit of their product equals zero.

Therefore, for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =\frac{1}{s+2\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s+2\text{i}}[{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-sa}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(-2a)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-2a))] \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2\text{i}}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2\text{i}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Laplace transform of ${e}^{-2\text{i}t}$ is $F(s)=\frac{1}{s+2\text{i}},$ defined for $s>0.$
